classification.difficultyReason: Apply tangent-radius perpendicularity to both circles, use a straight angle for external contact, and adapt the common-perpendicular argument to an internally touching drawing.

content.prompt: Prove that: When two circles touch, their centres and their point of contact are collinear.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Let two circles with centres O and P touch externally at T. Let ATB be the common tangent at T.

spec.description: Externally tangent circles at T. Common tangent ATB; centres O/P marked. No radii or centre line supplied.
spec.answerVisibility: Original supplied givens and targets only; no derived numerical values or proof conclusions.

answer.worked: Each radius is perpendicular to the tangent at its endpoint, so $\angle ATO=\angle ATP=90^\circ$.

children.label: ii
children.prompt: Hence, prove that O, T and P are collinear.

answer.short: O, T and P are collinear.
answer.worked: The externally touching circles lie on opposite sides of their common tangent. Thus $\angle OTP=\angle OTA+\angle ATP=90^\circ+90^\circ=180^\circ$. Therefore O, T and P are collinear.

children.label: b
children.prompt: Draw a diagram of two circles touching internally, and prove the theorem in this case.

answer.short: Both centres lie on the same perpendicular to the common tangent through the contact point.
answer.worked: Draw two internally touching circles and their common tangent ATB at T. Join each centre O and P to T. Both OT and PT are perpendicular to ATB at T. There is exactly one perpendicular through T to a given line, so O, P and T lie on the same line. The centres are on the same side of the tangent in this case.

spec.description: Example drawing: circle centre P radius2 and internal circle centre O radius1 touch at T; common tangent ATB. Centres/contact collinear.
